Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) is highly likely given prominent cutaneous and pulmonary infections (e.g., catalase-positive organisms like S. aureus, Aspergillus), granuloma formation (implied by recurrent non-healing lesions), and growth failure; flow cytometry (DHR test) would confirm. SCID is also highly probable—though often presenting earlier with severe viral/bacterial/fungal infections and failure to thrive—but survival to age 3 without transplant suggests leaky or atypical forms (e.g., IL2RG, JAK3, RAG hypomorphs). Hyper-IgE syndrome fits well: eczematoid dermatitis, staphylococcal skin abscesses, pneumonias with pneumatoceles, and growth delay are hallmark features; STAT3 deficiency is the most common form. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is plausible: eczema, recurrent sinopulmonary infections, thrombocytopenia (not yet reported but may be subclinical), and growth failure—though classic microthrombocytopenia and bleeding are expected, they can be subtle early on. IL-12/IFN-γ axis defects (e.g., IFNGR1 deficiency) are less common but fit: susceptibility to nontuberculous mycobacteria and Salmonella, chronic skin ulcers, fever, and failure to thrive—though mycobacterial infection isn’t explicitly mentioned, it may be underrecognized in young children.
